name: Omar Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Omar. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or parties. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the live-line crew, which means we work on lines while the power stays on, so a hospital or a factory doesn't have to go dark for us to fix something. We use insulated sticks and rubber gloves rated way above the voltage, and every move is slow and planned. Most days it's two of us up in an insulated bucket, one on the ground watching, swapping an insulator or a cross-arm on the north side of the network.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the focus. Live work is the closest thing to a chess game you get outdoors. I'm also the one who flies the inspection drone, so before a job I send it up the line and check the hardware on my tablet. What wears me down is the waiting, standing by for switching permission for an hour, and summer heat in full rubber. I live with my girlfriend Priya, she's a nurse on nights, and we've got about four months of money put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say I told you so to my mate Sean, because he's convinced robots are taking over next Tuesday. Online I'd maybe post something about how the hype cycle burned out. I follow a lot of tech stuff, so I'd have opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I use AI every day, for drone photo checks, for writing up job safety plans, even for meal planning with Priya's night shifts. If it stalls there, my job stays great and my life stays basically the same, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on the crew and push for my advanced drone licence, which lets me fly beyond line of sight. I'd keep using the AI tools to cut my paperwork. And I'd keep putting money into the joint account Priya and I opened for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A tiny bit bored. Live work is a safe job, and if AI stalls here, my job stays great and my life stays basically the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be disappointed. What were you hoping AI would do that it doesn't do here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly the drone side. I wanted it to look at a thousand photos of insulators and tell me the three that are cracked, every time, without me squinting at a tablet in the van. In this picture it gets halfway there and then just stops improving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Priya make of all your tech stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm a bit obsessed, which is fair. She sees AI tools in the hospital that are half-finished and annoying, so she's more sceptical than me. We joke that I'd marry the drone if I could.

say: The **hype cycle burned out**, and I'd say so online because I follow tech closely.
I'd tease my colleague **Sean**, who expects robots to take over any day now.
think: I'd be a bit **disappointed**, because I already use AI every day.
Line work stays a **safe, well-paid job**, so life carries on fine.
do: Get the **advanced drone licence** for flying beyond line of sight.
Keep using **AI tools** to cut the paperwork on safety plans.
Keep saving into the **joint house account** with his girlfriend Priya.
feel: **Calm** and a little **bored** by how little changes.
S0.quote: Live work is a safe job, and if AI stalls here, my job stays great and my life stays basically the same.
fieldNote: Omar is the rare worker who is **let down** by a plateau, because he wanted better tools.
His girlfriend Priya, a nurse, is **more sceptical** and acts as a check on his enthusiasm.
He frames his job as **secure** and his ambitions as being about tools, not escape.

steps.text: Get the advanced drone licence for beyond-line-of-sight flying
Use AI to draft live-line job safety plans every day
Keep paying into the joint house account with Priya

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, honestly. At work I'd tell people to get on the new tools early, because the ones who learn first get to shape how they're used. I'd probably post a few videos of the drone stuff too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job gets better, not smaller. The thinking work on our crew is the planning and the paperwork, and AI eating that leaves us more time up the pole. The people I'd worry for are the schedulers and the customer line staff in the main office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to test any AI that plans live-line jobs, because I already do that by hand and know where it goes wrong. I'd also look at the robot arms some companies are trialling for live work, and ask to go on a training trip. And I'd keep saving, maybe a bit harder, in case the overtime gets thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. There's a version of this where I end up being the crew's tech person and get paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overtime might get thinner. Why would that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI plans the jobs better, fewer jobs overrun and fewer of us get called in on a Saturday. Overtime is about a fifth of my pay, and better AI planning is good for safety and bad for my bank account. I'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dee in the control room. She takes the outage calls and juggles which crew goes where. In this picture a lot of that gets done by software, and I'm not sure where she goes.

say: This is the **good version**, so get on the new tools early.
I'd post **drone videos** online and encourage the crew to shape how tools are used.
think: My job gets **better, not smaller**, because AI takes the planning and paperwork.
**Schedulers and call staff** in the main office are the ones at risk.
do: Volunteer to **test the AI** that plans live-line jobs.
Ask to join a **training trip** on live-work robot arms.
Save a bit harder in case **overtime** gets thinner.
feel: **Calm** and a little **excited** about becoming the crew's tech person.
S1.quote: Overtime is about a fifth of my pay, and better AI planning is good for safety and bad for my bank account.
fieldNote: Omar sees **office jobs** taking the hit while his hands-on work gains time.
He spots a quiet **money risk**: overtime is about a fifth of his pay.
His instinct is to get **inside the change** by testing tools before they are imposed.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the AI tool that plans live-line jobs
Ask to join a training trip on live-work robot arms
Put an extra £150 a month aside to cover thinner overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three pictures share an end point. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it's going to be wild, and that line crews have three years more than most people. I'd say that in the group chat too. I'd try not to sound smug, because a lot of my mates work in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the three years are real but short. Live-line work is actually one of the first hands-on jobs utilities want robots for, because it's dangerous. So in 2031 I don't think robots replace every lineman, but I think they replace live-line crews like mine first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go after the robot side hard, asking to be trained on whatever robot the company buys. I'd also look at the drone inspection firms, because AI plus drones probably wipes out foot patrols. And I'd raise our savings from four months to six, which means no holiday next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I like my odds more than most, but there will be fewer robot-minder jobs than there are linemen now. Two years isn't much time to make sure I'm one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said live-line crews get replaced first. How sure are you about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not sure at all, it's a guess. But I've watched videos of the robot arms already working on live lines in a few countries, and they're clumsy now. Give the clumsy robot arms AGI brains and three years, and I'd bet on the robot over me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya talk about the night you heard this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whose job is safer, probably, and it's hers. Nursing is hands-on and people-facing, so I think she lasts longer than me. We'd talk about her being the steady income for a bit while I jump to whatever comes next.

say: It's going to be **wild**, and line crews get **three more years** than most.
I'd try not to sound **smug** to friends working in offices.
think: **Live-line work** is dangerous, so it's among the first hands-on jobs robots will target.
By **2031** I expect live-line crews like mine to go before regular linemen.
do: Ask to be trained on **whatever robot** the company buys.
Look at **drone inspection firms**, since AI plus drones could replace foot patrols.
Raise savings from four to **six months**, skipping next summer's holiday.
feel: **Anxious**, because there will be **fewer robot-minder jobs** than linemen today.
S2.quote: Give the clumsy robot arms AGI brains and three years, and I'd bet on the robot over me.
fieldNote: Omar thinks his own **specialism** is more exposed than ordinary line work, a surprising self-assessment.
He sees his girlfriend's **nursing job** as the household's safer income.
Even as an early adopter, he admits two years is **too little time** to secure a place.

steps.text: Ask to be first trained on any live-line robot the company buys
Apply to drone inspection firms within the first year
Skip next summer's holiday to reach six months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it, if you start now. At work I'd push the company to set up a robotics team from the crews instead of hiring tech people from outside. I'd probably write a long post about it, Priya would roll her eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm okay here. By 2034, when the robots come, I'd be thirty-five with five or six years of robot and drone experience. That's the person a company hires to run a fleet of these things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a part-time course in robotics maintenance, about two evenings a week for two years. I'd keep flying the drone and log every hour, because hours are what employers check. And Priya and I would buy a small house in year two, because I'd feel confident about my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than scared. The fast one made me nervous; this one feels like a ladder I can climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd push for a robotics team from the crews. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the crews know where things go wrong. A tech graduate can programme a robot arm, but they don't know that a cracked insulator on a frosty morning can drop a line on you. I'd rather the machines learn from people who've been up the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a house in year two. What if you're wrong about your income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Priya's wage carries the mortgage on its own, which is why we'd buy small. We'd stretch to about three and a half times her salary, not ours together. That's our rule.

say: Five years is **enough to get ahead** if you start now.
The company should build a **robotics team** from the crews, not hire outsiders.
think: At **thirty-five** in 2034, I'd have years of **robot and drone** experience.
That makes me the kind of person a company hires to **run a fleet** of machines.
do: Take a **part-time robotics maintenance** course, two evenings a week for two years.
Log every **drone flight hour**, because employers check hours.
Buy a **small house** in year two, sized to his girlfriend Priya's wage alone.
feel: **Uneasy** but more **excited** than scared; it feels like a ladder.
S3.quote: A tech graduate can programme a robot arm, but they don't know that a cracked insulator on a frosty morning can drop a line on you.
fieldNote: With five years, Omar moves from fear to **planning a career step** into robot fleets.
He insists crews should **teach the machines**, which mixes pride and self-interest.
The mortgage rule built on **one income** shows a cautious streak behind the enthusiasm.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year part-time robotics maintenance course
Buy a small house sized to Priya's nursing wage alone
Ask the union and managers to staff robot teams from line crews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, and anyone in my trade who ignores it has only themselves to blame. I'd say that kindly, but I'd say it. Then I'd go back to arguing about which robot company will win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is the version where I come out ahead. I'd have time to become properly good at robotics, maybe even start something of my own on the side. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine, which is a good age to be running a team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course without rushing, and I'd start a small drone inspection side business on weekends, checking solar roofs and farm sheds. If it works, that's a second income before the robots ever arrive. Priya and I would buy the house and maybe think about kids around year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. There's always the chance I'm wrong about which jobs survive, but ten years is a long time to fix a wrong guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a side business. How would that actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the money from the advanced licence course to buy a decent second drone, about three thousand pounds. Then I'd ask the farmers out past the reservoir if they want their barn roofs checked after storms. I already have the AI software to spot damage in the photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about, even in this slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, actually. He drives a delivery van, and he's fifty-five. Ten years for him is retirement age right when the robots turn up, and he's not someone who'll retrain. I'd want to help him get to the finish line.

say: Ten years is **loads of time**, so anyone in the trade who ignores it is to blame.
I'd say that **kindly**, then go back to debating which **robot company** wins.
think: This is the version where I **come out ahead** with real robotics skills.
At **thirty-nine** in 2039, I'd be the right age to run a team.
do: Start a weekend **drone inspection** side business for solar roofs and farm sheds.
Take the **robotics course** at a relaxed pace.
Buy a house with Priya and think about **kids** around year four.
feel: **Calm**, with a small worry about **guessing wrong** on which jobs survive.
S4.quote: There's always the chance I'm wrong about which jobs survive, but ten years is a long time to fix a wrong guess.
fieldNote: With a decade, Omar plans a **second income** through drone inspections before robots arrive.
His main worry shifts to his **father**, a 55-year-old van driver unlikely to retrain.
He blames workers who **ignore warnings**, a pragmatic rather than political view.

steps.text: Buy a £3,000 second drone and inspect farm roofs on weekends
Take the robotics maintenance course at a relaxed pace
Buy a house with Priya and plan for children around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd probably land on my feet, but live-line crews are first in line for robots, and two years isn't enough to make sure. What would help is the company training crews on robots before they buy them, and a straight answer about how many robot-minder jobs there will be.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me actually want the robots. I do, partly, because live work kills people every year. A robot that takes the dangerous jobs and leaves me running it is the best outcome, if there's still a me in the picture.

headlineQuote: A robot that takes the dangerous jobs and leaves me running it is the best outcome, if there's still a me in the picture.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old live-line worker** and the crew's drone pilot, living with his girlfriend Priya, a nurse.
He uses AI **every day** and is mildly disappointed by a world where it stalls.
He thinks **live-line crews** are first in line for robots because the work is so dangerous.
Given time, he plans to **run robot fleets** and build a drone inspection side business.
He keeps a cautious rule of buying a house on **one income** in case he guesses wrong.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years may not be enough to secure a robot-minder job.
whatWouldHelp: Training crews on **robots before purchase**, and an honest count of future robot-minder jobs.
